title: How states can slow the staffing surge
author: Aaron Garth Smith
source: The Thomas B. Fordham Institute (fordhaminstitute.org), September 24, 2026
summary: Aaron Garth Smith of the Reason Foundation argues that record school funding has not reached teacher paychecks because districts keep adding non-teaching staff. Between 2002 and 2023, real per-student funding rose 36 percent while inflation-adjusted teacher salaries fell and non-teaching staff grew 23 percent. His remedy has two parts. First, states should decentralize spending by eliminating categorical grants that fund specific support positions, scrutinizing community-school appropriations, repealing staffing-ratio mandates, and giving principals authority to convert positions into compensation dollars. Second, they should modernize teacher pay by ending mandated master's degree premiums, loosening collective bargaining constraints, and expanding performance and shortage-area pay on models like Texas's Teacher Incentive Allotment. Smith even floats Principal Empowerment Accounts that send money directly to principals to reward their best teachers.
points: From 2002 to 2023, real per-student funding rose 36 percent while average inflation-adjusted teacher pay fell and non-teaching staff grew 23 percent.
State categorical grants and staffing-ratio mandates, such as Virginia's counselor and librarian ratios, lock districts into adding positions rather than raising pay.
Research shows teachers with advanced degrees are generally no more effective, yet nearly a third of states mandate master's degree pay premiums.
Texas's Teacher Incentive Allotment offers early evidence that performance pay can improve retention and achievement.
Smith proposes Principal Empowerment Accounts, modeled on Great Hearts' Teacher Excellence Fund, to let principals directly reward top teachers.
quotes: Public schools are increasingly spending more outside the classroom, with non-teaching staff—such as instructional aides, counselors, and social workers—increasing by 23 percent.
But it’s a real problem, given that research shows teachers are the most important in-school factor affecting student outcomes, underscoring the significant opportunity costs of this spending.

Requiring school districts to spend a minimum portion of their funding on teacher compensation, as Indiana does, might be tempting. But money is fungible, and no single way to allocate resources is optimal for every school district.
But one-size-fits-all grants prevent local leaders from making tradeoffs between higher compensation, additional staffing, and other uses of scarce resources.
As it stands, most school budgets revolve around staffing positions, incentivizing school leaders to advocate for additional full-time equivalents (FTEs) rather than higher teacher salaries.

While research indicates that teachers tend to improve with experience (with diminishing returns after the first ten years or so), studies show that teachers with advanced degrees are generally no more effective than teachers with bachelor’s degrees.
This might sound radical, but principals in private schools and charters routinely have more discretion over teacher pay than their public school counterparts.
